claim: The actomyosin ring generates force to ingress the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in animal cells.
source: The actomyosin ring generates force to ingress the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in animal cells, yet its filament organization and the mechanism of contractility is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about the actomyosin ring's function.

claim: The filament organization and mechanism of contractility of the actomyosin ring is not well understood.
source: The actomyosin ring generates force to ingress the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in animal cells, yet its filament organization and the mechanism of contractility is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cleavage furrow ingression initiates by contraction of an equatorial actin network with randomly oriented filaments.
source: We quantified actin filament order in human cells using fluorescence polarization microscopy and found that cleavage furrow ingression initiates by contraction of an equatorial actin network with randomly oriented filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization microscopy measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The actin network subsequently gradually reoriented actin filaments along the cell equator.
source: The network subsequently gradually reoriented actin filaments along the cell equator.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved fluorescence polarization microscopy data.

claim: Actin filament reorientation strictly depends on myosin II activity.
source: This strictly depended on myosin II activity, suggesting local network reorganization by mechanical forces.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using myosin II inhibitor para-nitroblebbistatin.

claim: Myosin II-dependent actin filament reorientation suggests local network reorganization by mechanical forces.
source: This strictly depended on myosin II activity, suggesting local network reorganization by mechanical forces.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the myosin II inhibition experiments.

claim: During cytokinesis progression, mechanical tension increased substantially along the direction of the cell equator.
source: Cortical laser microsurgery revealed that during cytokinesis progression, mechanical tension increased substantially along the direction of the cell equator, while the network contracted laterally along the pole-to-pole axis without a detectable increase in tension.
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery experiments measuring cortical displacement.

claim: The network contracted laterally along the pole-to-pole axis without a detectable increase in tension.
source: Cortical laser microsurgery revealed that during cytokinesis progression, mechanical tension increased substantially along the direction of the cell equator, while the network contracted laterally along the pole-to-pole axis without a detectable increase in tension.
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery experiments showing no significant tension increase along the pole-to-pole axis.

claim: An asymmetric increase in cortical tension promotes filament reorientation along the cytokinetic cleavage furrow.
source: Our data suggest that an asymmetric increase in cortical tension promotes filament reorientation along the cytokinetic cleavage furrow, which might have implications for diverse other biological processes involving actomyosin rings.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the tension and filament orientation measurements.

claim: Animal cells divide by contracting the cell cortex in an equatorial zone between the two poles of the mitotic spindle.
source: Animal cells divide by contracting the cell cortex in an equatorial zone between the two poles of the mitotic spindle, resulting in the ingression of a cleavage furrow.
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal cell division.

claim: Cortex contraction results in the ingression of a cleavage furrow.
source: Animal cells divide by contracting the cell cortex in an equatorial zone between the two poles of the mitotic spindle, resulting in the ingression of a cleavage furrow.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequence of cortex contraction.

claim: Cleavage furrow formation is initiated by activation of the small GTPase RhoA at the equatorial cell cortex.
source: This is initiated by activation of the small GTPase RhoA at the equatorial cell cortex, which induces polymerization of unbranched actin filaments and activation of non-muscle myosin II (Piekny et al., 2005; Bement et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RhoA activation induces polymerization of unbranched actin filaments.
source: This is initiated by activation of the small GTPase RhoA at the equatorial cell cortex, which induces polymerization of unbranched actin filaments and activation of non-muscle myosin II (Piekny et al., 2005; Bement et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RhoA activation induces activation of non-muscle myosin II.
source: This is initiated by activation of the small GTPase RhoA at the equatorial cell cortex, which induces polymerization of unbranched actin filaments and activation of non-muscle myosin II (Piekny et al., 2005; Bement et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The actomyosin ring was discovered more than four decades ago.
source: The equatorial zone of actin and myosin enrichment, termed the actomyosin ring, was discovered more than four decades ago (Schroeder, 1968; Schroeder, 1972), yet how its filaments organize to generate contractile force remains poorly understood (Eggert et al., 2006; Green et al., 2012; Fededa and Gerlich, 2012; Cheffings et al., 2016; Wang, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical research.

claim: How actomyosin ring filaments organize to generate contractile force remains poorly understood.
source: The equatorial zone of actin and myosin enrichment, termed the actomyosin ring, was discovered more than four decades ago (Schroeder, 1968; Schroeder, 1972), yet how its filaments organize to generate contractile force remains poorly understood (Eggert et al., 2006; Green et al., 2012; Fededa and Gerlich, 2012; Cheffings et al., 2016; Wang, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles discussing the state of knowledge.

claim: Electron microscopy revealed that many actin filaments orient along the edge of the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in marine embryos.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that many actin filaments orient along the edge of the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in marine embryos (Schroeder, 1972; Henson et al., 2017) and vertebrate cells (Maupin and Pollard, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Electron microscopy revealed that many actin filaments orient along the edge of the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in vertebrate cells.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that many actin filaments orient along the edge of the cytokinetic cleavage furrow in marine embryos (Schroeder, 1972; Henson et al., 2017) and vertebrate cells (Maupin and Pollard, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: The actomyosin ring might contract by anti-parallel filament sliding similar to muscle sarcomeres.
source: This led to the suggestion that the actomyosin ring might contract by anti-parallel filament sliding similar to muscle sarcomeres (Schroeder, 1972).
evidence: This is a historical model cited from prior research.

claim: Actin filament alignment during the initiation of furrow ingression appears less prominent.
source: The actin filament alignment during the initiation of furrow ingression, however, appears less prominent (Mabuchi, 1994; Fishkind and Wang, 1993; Noguchi and Mabuchi, 2001; DeBiasio et al., 1996; Fenix et al., 2016) and whether the filament sliding model appropriately describes animal cell cytokinesis has remained under debate (Eggert et al., 2006; Green et al., 2012; Fededa and Gerlich, 2012; Cheffings et al., 2016; Wang, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Whether the filament sliding model appropriately describes animal cell cytokinesis has remained under debate.
source: The actin filament alignment during the initiation of furrow ingression, however, appears less prominent (Mabuchi, 1994; Fishkind and Wang, 1993; Noguchi and Mabuchi, 2001; DeBiasio et al., 1996; Fenix et al., 2016) and whether the filament sliding model appropriately describes animal cell cytokinesis has remained under debate (Eggert et al., 2006; Green et al., 2012; Fededa and Gerlich, 2012; Cheffings et al., 2016; Wang, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In vitro experiments showed that disorganized actomyosin networks can generate contractile force.
source: In vitro experiments showed that disorganized actomyosin networks can also generate contractile force (Pollard, 1976; Janson et al., 1991; Murrell et al., 2015; Linsmeier et al., 2016; Ennomani et al., 2016), which is explained by the imbalance of tensile over compressive forces that can be transduced by actin filaments (Murrell et al., 2015; Linsmeier et al., 2016; Murrell and Gardel, 2012; Vogel et al., 2013; Lenz et al., 2012; Lenz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vitro experimental studies.

claim: Contractile force generation in disorganized actomyosin networks is explained by the imbalance of tensile over compressive forces that can be transduced by actin filaments.
source: In vitro experiments showed that disorganized actomyosin networks can also generate contractile force (Pollard, 1976; Janson et al., 1991; Murrell et al., 2015; Linsmeier et al., 2016; Ennomani et al., 2016), which is explained by the imbalance of tensile over compressive forces that can be transduced by actin filaments (Murrell et al., 2015; Linsmeier et al., 2016; Murrell and Gardel, 2012; Vogel et al., 2013; Lenz et al., 2012; Lenz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: It is possible that the actomyosin ring ingresses by network contraction rather than sliding of anti-parallel filament bundles.
source: It is therefore possible that the actomyosin ring ingresses by network contraction rather than sliding of anti-parallel filament bundles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the in vitro findings cited.

claim: Theoretical models suggest that actin filament alignment during cytokinesis might be a consequence rather than cause of actomyosin contractility.
source: Theoretical models suggest that actin filament alignment during cytokinesis might be a consequence rather than cause of actomyosin contractility (Greenspan, 1977; White and Borisy, 1983; Bray and White, 1988; Zinemanas and Nir, 1988; Verkhovsky et al., 1999; Salbreux et al., 2009; Stachowiak et al., 2014; Dorn et al., 2016; Reymann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical modeling studies.

claim: In large cells of Caenorhabditis elegans early embryos, actin filament alignment is driven by a myosin-dependent long-range cortical flow that precedes furrow ingression.
source: In large cells of Caenorhabditis elegans early embryos, actin filament alignment is driven by a myosin-dependent long-range cortical flow that precedes furrow ingression (Reymann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on C. elegans.

claim: In fission yeast, actin filaments nucleate at discrete loci that interact and contract to align filaments at the cell equator.
source: In fission yeast, actin filaments nucleate at discrete loci that interact and contract to align filaments at the cell equator (Stachowiak et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2006; Vavylonis et al., 2008; Kamasaki et al., 2007; Laplante et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fission yeast.

claim: Dividing vertebrate cells do not have prominent actin nucleation foci.
source: Dividing vertebrate cells do not have prominent actin nucleation foci and they have less pronounced cortical flow compared to large embryo cells (Cao and Wang, 1990; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005; Zhou and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on vertebrate cells.

claim: Dividing vertebrate cells have less pronounced cortical flow compared to large embryo cells.
source: Dividing vertebrate cells do not have prominent actin nucleation foci and they have less pronounced cortical flow compared to large embryo cells (Cao and Wang, 1990; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005; Zhou and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies comparing vertebrate cells to embryo cells.

claim: It has remained unclear how myosin-mediated contractility contributes to filament organization within the actomyosin ring of vertebrate cells.
source: It has thus remained unclear how myosin-mediated contractility contributes to filament organization within the actomyosin ring of vertebrate cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The direct visualization of filament orientation within the actomyosin ring is difficult owing to the resolution limit of light microscopes.
source: The direct visualization of filament orientation within the actomyosin ring is difficult owing to the resolution limit of light microscopes and potential fixation and staining artifacts in electron microscopy.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations in microscopy.

claim: The direct visualization of filament orientation within the actomyosin ring is difficult owing to potential fixation and staining artifacts in electron microscopy.
source: The direct visualization of filament orientation within the actomyosin ring is difficult owing to the resolution limit of light microscopes and potential fixation and staining artifacts in electron microscopy.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations in electron microscopy.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy provides an approach to quantify filament orientation independently of the resolution limit of the microscope.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy, however, provides an alternative approach to quantify filament orientation independently of the resolution limit of the microscope, by reporting the net orientation of fluorophore dipoles bound to filaments (DeMay et al., 2011a; McQuilken et al., 2015; Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fluorescence polarization microscopy studies.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy reports the net orientation of fluorophore dipoles bound to filaments.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy, however, provides an alternative approach to quantify filament orientation independently of the resolution limit of the microscope, by reporting the net orientation of fluorophore dipoles bound to filaments (DeMay et al., 2011a; McQuilken et al., 2015; Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations explaining the principle of fluorescence polarization microscopy.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy revealed septin filament reorientations in the bud neck of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy indeed revealed septin filament reorientations in the bud neck of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DeMay et al., 2011b; Vrabioiu and Mitchison, 2006), actin filament anisotropy during cytokinesis of vertebrate cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993) and Drosophila embryos, (Mavrakis et al., 2014) and dynamic orientation of actin filaments within the lamellipodium of migrating cells (Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fluorescence polarization microscopy studies.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy revealed actin filament anisotropy during cytokinesis of vertebrate cells.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy indeed revealed septin filament reorientations in the bud neck of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DeMay et al., 2011b; Vrabioiu and Mitchison, 2006), actin filament anisotropy during cytokinesis of vertebrate cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993) and Drosophila embryos, (Mavrakis et al., 2014) and dynamic orientation of actin filaments within the lamellipodium of migrating cells (Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy revealed actin filament anisotropy during cytokinesis of Drosophila embryos.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy indeed revealed septin filament reorientations in the bud neck of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DeMay et al., 2011b; Vrabioiu and Mitchison, 2006), actin filament anisotropy during cytokinesis of vertebrate cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993) and Drosophila embryos, (Mavrakis et al., 2014) and dynamic orientation of actin filaments within the lamellipodium of migrating cells (Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy revealed dynamic orientation of actin filaments within the lamellipodium of migrating cells.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy indeed revealed septin filament reorientations in the bud neck of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DeMay et al., 2011b; Vrabioiu and Mitchison, 2006), actin filament anisotropy during cytokinesis of vertebrate cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993) and Drosophila embryos, (Mavrakis et al., 2014) and dynamic orientation of actin filaments within the lamellipodium of migrating cells (Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Prior fluorescence polarization microscopy analysis showed an increase of actin filament alignment at late stages of cytokinesis in mammalian cells.
source: While prior fluorescence polarization microscopy analysis showed an increase of actin filament alignment at late stages of cytokinesis in mammalian cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993), the precise timing and absolute degree of actomyosin network order during cytokinesis, the distribution of forces during cytokinesis progression, and the mechanisms underlying actin filament alignment have remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The precise timing and absolute degree of actomyosin network order during cytokinesis have remained unclear.
source: While prior fluorescence polarization microscopy analysis showed an increase of actin filament alignment at late stages of cytokinesis in mammalian cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993), the precise timing and absolute degree of actomyosin network order during cytokinesis, the distribution of forces during cytokinesis progression, and the mechanisms underlying actin filament alignment have remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in knowledge.

claim: The distribution of forces during cytokinesis progression has remained unclear.
source: While prior fluorescence polarization microscopy analysis showed an increase of actin filament alignment at late stages of cytokinesis in mammalian cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993), the precise timing and absolute degree of actomyosin network order during cytokinesis, the distribution of forces during cytokinesis progression, and the mechanisms underlying actin filament alignment have remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in knowledge.

claim: The mechanisms underlying actin filament alignment have remained unclear.
source: While prior fluorescence polarization microscopy analysis showed an increase of actin filament alignment at late stages of cytokinesis in mammalian cells (Fishkind and Wang, 1993), the precise timing and absolute degree of actomyosin network order during cytokinesis, the distribution of forces during cytokinesis progression, and the mechanisms underlying actin filament alignment have remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in knowledge.

claim: Alexa488-phalloidin binds to F-actin filaments with defined orientation of the fluorophore dipoles.
source: Alexa488-phalloidin was previously shown to bind to F-actin filaments with defined orientation of the fluorophore dipoles (Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The LC-PolScope enables analysis of fluorophore orientation and therefore the orientation of actin filaments.
source: The LC-PolScope enables to analyze the orientation of these fluorophores and therefore the orientation of the actin filaments.
evidence: This is a statement about the capability of the LC-PolScope technique.

claim: The liquid crystal modulates the linear polarization direction of the excitation laser into four different angles.
source: To this end, the liquid crystal modulates the linear polarization direction of the excitation laser into four different angles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the technical setup, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Maximally anisotropic fluorophore orientation is expected for parallel filaments that are aligned with the optical section.
source: Maximally anisotropic fluorophore orientation is expected for parallel filaments that are aligned with the optical section (Figure 1A 'parallel view').
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation illustrated in a figure.

claim: The normalized polarization factor for stress fibers is close to 1.
source: We then normalized the polarization factor to be in a range between 1 and 0 for maximally aligned fluorophores in stress fibers and randomly oriented fluorophores in plastic, respectively.
evidence: This is implied by the normalization procedure described and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The normalized polarization factor for randomly oriented fluorophores in plastic is 0.
source: We then normalized the polarization factor to be in a range between 1 and 0 for maximally aligned fluorophores in stress fibers and randomly oriented fluorophores in plastic, respectively.
evidence: This is stated explicitly and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The normalized polarization factor of metaphase cells is 0.57 ± 0.09.
source: The detected normalized polarization factor of 0.57 ± 0.09 (Figure 1C; median ±s.d., as for all following measurements) was indeed close to the value expected for a thin isotropic actin network in metaphase cells, indicating that the confocal LC-PolScope is suitable for quantitative analysis of degree of filament order within actin networks.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The normalized polarization factor of 0.57 ± 0.09 in metaphase cells is close to the value expected for a thin isotropic actin network.
source: The detected normalized polarization factor of 0.57 ± 0.09 (Figure 1C; median ±s.d., as for all following measurements) was indeed close to the value expected for a thin isotropic actin network in metaphase cells, indicating that the confocal LC-PolScope is suitable for quantitative analysis of degree of filament order within actin networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured value.

claim: The confocal LC-PolScope is suitable for quantitative analysis of degree of filament order within actin networks.
source: The detected normalized polarization factor of 0.57 ± 0.09 (Figure 1C; median ±s.d., as for all following measurements) was indeed close to the value expected for a thin isotropic actin network in metaphase cells, indicating that the confocal LC-PolScope is suitable for quantitative analysis of degree of filament order within actin networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation measurements.

claim: At late stages of cytokinesis, there is a pronounced reduction of the normalized polarization factor at the cell equator.
source: At late stages of cytokinesis, we indeed observed a pronounced reduction of the normalized polarization factor at the cell equator (Figures 1E, 201-300 s, cortex area with low-color saturation; quantification in 1F), consistent with preferential orientation of actin filaments along the cell equator.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: The reduction of the normalized polarization factor at the cell equator is consistent with preferential orientation of actin filaments along the cell equator.
source: At late stages of cytokinesis, we indeed observed a pronounced reduction of the normalized polarization factor at the cell equator (Figures 1E, 201-300 s, cortex area with low-color saturation; quantification in 1F), consistent with preferential orientation of actin filaments along the cell equator.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the polarization measurements.

claim: The reduction of the normalized polarization factor at the cell equator cannot be attributed to higher levels of mean Alexa488-phalloidin fluorescence.
source: The reduction of the normalized polarization factor at the cell equator cannot be attributed to the higher levels of mean Alexa488-phalloidin fluorescence, as fluctuations of mean fluorescence along the cell cortex did not correlate with the degree of polarization at early cytokinesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Following the onset of chromosome segregation, anaphase cells start to ingress a cleavage furrow after 101–150 s.
source: Following the onset of chromosome segregation in an almost spherical cell, anaphase cells start to ingress a cleavage furrow after 101–150 s, visible as a curvature reduction at the equator (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on staging of cells shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At early furrow ingression states, the normalized polarization factor is indistinguishable between equator and pole.
source: At these early furrow ingression states, the normalized polarization factor was indistinguishable between equator and pole (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1G.

claim: At later furrow ingression states (151–300 s), the normalized polarization factor at the cleavage furrow decreased significantly compared to the pole and the initial metaphase values.
source: Only at later furrow ingression states (151–300 s), the normalized polarization factor at the cleavage furrow decreased significantly compared to the pole and the initial metaphase values (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1G with statistical testing.

claim: There is a small increase of normalized polarization factor at the poles during late stages of cytokinesis.
source: We also noticed a small increase of normalized polarization factor at the poles during late stages of cytokinesis, which might reflect cortical reorganization when cells reattach to the glass substratum during mitotic exit.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The increase of normalized polarization factor at the poles might reflect cortical reorganization when cells reattach to the glass substratum during mitotic exit.
source: We also noticed a small increase of normalized polarization factor at the poles during late stages of cytokinesis, which might reflect cortical reorganization when cells reattach to the glass substratum during mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation.

claim: The orientation of actin filaments in the equatorial network driving initial stages of constriction is indistinguishable from the random orientation observed in the cortex of metaphase cells.
source: Overall, these observations indicate that the orientation of actin filaments in the equatorial network driving initial stages of constriction is indistinguishable from the random orientation observed in the cortex of metaphase cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the polarization measurements at different stages.

claim: Fluorescent phalloidin cannot be used for live-cell imaging because it does not passage the plasma membrane.
source: Fluorescent phalloidin cannot be used for this purpose, as it does not passage the plasma membrane and is known to be highly toxic.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of phalloidin.

claim: Fluorescent phalloidin is highly toxic.
source: Fluorescent phalloidin cannot be used for this purpose, as it does not passage the plasma membrane and is known to be highly toxic.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of phalloidin.

claim: SiR-actin is a plasma membrane-permeant, fluorogenic actin marker that has low toxicity.
source: We thus tested a silicone rhodamine-coupled jasplakinolide derivate, SiR-actin, which is a plasma membrane-permeant, fluorogenic actin marker that has low toxicity (Lukinavičius et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: SiR-actin generates a strong polarization-dependent signal on stress fibers of live hTERT-RPE-1 cells.
source: SiR-actin indeed generated a strong polarization-dependent signal on stress fibers of live hTERT-RPE-1 cells (Figure 2A), and it did not impair the efficiency and rate of cleavage furrow ingression at the concentration used for imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SiR-actin does not impair the efficiency and rate of cleavage furrow ingression at the concentration used for imaging.
source: SiR-actin indeed generated a strong polarization-dependent signal on stress fibers of live hTERT-RPE-1 cells (Figure 2A), and it did not impair the efficiency and rate of cleavage furrow ingression at the concentration used for imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Significant inward-directed curvature changes at the equator are detected at 90 s post anaphase onset.
source: We detected significant inward-directed curvature changes at 90 s post anaphase onset (Figure 2E; n = 18 movies).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Significant changes in equatorial emission ratio of SiR-actin occur at 120 s after anaphase onset.
source: Quantification of the equatorial emission ratio of SiR-actin in the same data set revealed significant changes only at 120 s after anaphase onset (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Furrow initiation precedes detectable changes in equatorial actin network orientation in vertebrate cells.
source: Thus, furrow initiation precedes detectable changes in equatorial actin network orientation in vertebrate cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the timing of curvature changes versus emission ratio changes.

claim: The actin cortex in metaphase cells is thinner than in interphase cells.
source: We found that the actin cortex in metaphase cells is thinner than in interphase cells, consistent with prior findings (Chugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by measurements and citation to a prior study.

claim: There is no significant difference between the thickness of the equatorial cortex of metaphase and anaphase cells.
source: Importantly, however, we did not detect a significant difference between the thickness of the equatorial cortex of metaphase and anaphase cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), indicating that equatorial actin accumulations in anaphase cells must be due to increased local filament density.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Equatorial actin accumulations in anaphase cells are due to increased local filament density.
source: Importantly, however, we did not detect a significant difference between the thickness of the equatorial cortex of metaphase and anaphase cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), indicating that equatorial actin accumulations in anaphase cells must be due to increased local filament density.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cortex thickness measurements.

claim: The equatorial fluorescence anisotropy changes detected during cytokinesis progression cannot be attributed to cortical thickening.
source: The equatorial fluorescence anisotropy changes detected during cytokinesis progression hence cannot be attributed to cortical thickening.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cortex thickness measurements.

claim: Blebbistatin is a specific inhibitor of non-muscle myosin II that suppresses cleavage furrow ingression.
source: Blebbistatin is a specific inhibitor of non-muscle myosin II that suppresses cleavage furrow ingression but does not prevent accumulation of actin and myosin II at the equatorial cell cortex (Zhou and Wang, 2008; Straight et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Blebbistatin does not prevent accumulation of actin and myosin II at the equatorial cell cortex.
source: Blebbistatin is a specific inhibitor of non-muscle myosin II that suppresses cleavage furrow ingression but does not prevent accumulation of actin and myosin II at the equatorial cell cortex (Zhou and Wang, 2008; Straight et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Para-nitroblebbistatin is a more photostable version of blebbistatin.
source: Para-nitroblebbistatin is a more photostable version of this inhibitor (Képiró et al., 2014), and it completely suppressed cleavage furrow ingression in hTERT-RPE-1 cells (Figure 2B, 'Blebbistatin' and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Para-nitroblebbistatin completely suppresses cleavage furrow ingression in hTERT-RPE-1 cells.
source: Para-nitroblebbistatin is a more photostable version of this inhibitor (Képiró et al., 2014), and it completely suppressed cleavage furrow ingression in hTERT-RPE-1 cells (Figure 2B, 'Blebbistatin' and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Actin filament accumulation at the cell equator is not affected in blebbistatin-treated cells.
source: Actin filament accumulation at the cell equator was not affected in blebbistatin-treated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C), yet emission ratio changes of SiR-actin at the equator were completely suppressed. (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Emission ratio changes of SiR-actin at the equator are completely suppressed in blebbistatin-treated cells.
source: Actin filament accumulation at the cell equator was not affected in blebbistatin-treated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C), yet emission ratio changes of SiR-actin at the equator were completely suppressed. (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Myosin II activity is not required for equatorial actin filament accumulation but is essential for filament reorientation along the cell circumference.
source: Thus, myosin II activity is not required for equatorial actin filament accumulation but is essential for filament reorientation along the cell circumference.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blebbistatin experiments.

claim: Myosin II enriches at the cell cortex along a gradient that peaks at the cleavage furrow, with a full width at half maximum of 4.3 ± 0.9 µm.
source: Myosin II enriched at the cell cortex along a gradient that peaked at the cleavage furrow, with a full width at half maximum of 4.3 ± 0.9 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: The myosin II distribution closely matches the lateral distribution of anisotropy within the actin network (4.4 ± 1.5 μm).
source: This distribution closely matched the lateral distribution of anisotropy within the actin network (4.4 ± 1.5 μm, see Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a comparison of measurements from different figures.

claim: The peak of SiR-actin fluorescence localizes to the cell equator with a full width at half maximum of 8.4 ± 1.8 μm.
source: The peak of SiR-actin fluorescence also localized to the cell equator, but the distribution was substantially broader, with a full width at half maximum of 8.4 ± 1.8 μm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: Equatorial accumulation and reorientation of actin filaments within the cortex are distinctly regulated.
source: Together, our data indicate that equatorial accumulation and reorientation of actin filaments within the cortex are distinctly regulated, supporting a model of myosin-mediated actin network reorganization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the myosin II inhibition and localization experiments.

claim: Confined cells form a cleavage furrow in the x-y optical plane but are substantially delayed toward ingression along the z-axis.
source: Confined cells formed a cleavage furrow in the x-y optical plane (Figure 3B–D) but were substantially delayed toward ingression along the z-axis (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: In confined cells, actin filaments accumulate at the cell equator at about 90 s after anaphase onset.
source: Actin filaments accumulated at the cell equator at about 90 s after anaphase onset (Figure 3E and F), and SiR-actin normalized emission ratio measurements began to increase at about 120 s after anaphase onset (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: In confined cells, SiR-actin normalized emission ratio measurements begin to increase at about 120 s after anaphase onset.
source: Actin filaments accumulated at the cell equator at about 90 s after anaphase onset (Figure 3E and F), and SiR-actin normalized emission ratio measurements began to increase at about 120 s after anaphase onset (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Concomitant with the equatorial accumulation of LifeAct-mCherry, there is minimal lateral displacement of cortical actin filaments toward the equator.
source: Concomitant with the equatorial accumulation of LifeAct-mCherry, we observed a minimal lateral displacement of cortical actin filaments toward the equator (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Minimal lateral displacement of cortical actin filaments argues against a strong contribution of 'cortical flow' in equatorial actin enrichment.
source: This argues against a strong contribution of 'cortical flow' of actin filaments in the equatorial actin enrichment and rather indicates that most actin filaments polymerize locally at the equator of somatic human cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the minimal lateral displacement observation.

claim: Most actin filaments polymerize locally at the equator of somatic human cells.
source: This argues against a strong contribution of 'cortical flow' of actin filaments in the equatorial actin enrichment and rather indicates that most actin filaments polymerize locally at the equator of somatic human cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the minimal lateral displacement observation.

claim: In metaphase cells, the cortical tension along the direction of the cell equator is approximately equal to the tension along the pole-to-pole axis.
source: In metaphase cells, the initial outward movement, and therefore the cortical tension along the direction of the cell equator, was approximately equal to the tension along the pole-to-pole axis (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery measurements shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: During early anaphase at pre-furrow ingression stages, cortical tension is similar to metaphase.
source: During early anaphase at pre-furrow ingression stages, cortical tension was similar as in metaphase, but it increased significantly along the direction of the cell equator once the cleavage furrow had begun to ingress (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery measurements shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Cortical tension increases significantly along the direction of the cell equator once the cleavage furrow has begun to ingress.
source: During early anaphase at pre-furrow ingression stages, cortical tension was similar as in metaphase, but it increased significantly along the direction of the cell equator once the cleavage furrow had begun to ingress (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery measurements shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: During late furrow ingression stages, cortical tension further increases along the direction of the cell equator.
source: During late furrow ingression stages, cortical tension further increased along the direction of the cell equator.
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery measurements.

claim: Along the pole-to-pole axis, cortical tension remains as low as in metaphase during all stages of cytokinesis.
source: Along the pole-to-pole axis, however, cortical tension remained as low as in metaphase during all stages of cytokinesis (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by laser microsurgery measurements shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The contractility of the actomyosin ring generates cortical tension predominantly along the direction of the cell equator.
source: Together, these data show that the contractility of the actomyosin ring generates cortical tension predominantly along the direction of the cell equator.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the directional tension measurements.

claim: A randomly organized actin network at the bottom surface of confined metaphase cells becomes increasingly more aligned at later stages of cytokinesis.
source: We detected a randomly organized actin network at the bottom surface of confined metaphase cells that became increasingly more aligned at later stages of cytokinesis (Figure 4I), correlating with an increase in cortical tension along the cell equator (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Actin network alignment correlates with an increase in cortical tension along the cell equator.
source: We detected a randomly organized actin network at the bottom surface of confined metaphase cells that became increasingly more aligned at later stages of cytokinesis (Figure 4I), correlating with an increase in cortical tension along the cell equator (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Laser-cutting the actin network perpendicular to the cell equator does not cause significant fluorescence polarization changes adjacent to the cut region at any measured cell cycle stage.
source: Importantly, we did not detect significant fluorescence polarization changes induced by laser-cutting at any of the measured cell cycle stages (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Maintenance of equatorial actin filament alignment does not require persistent tension.
source: Thus, maintenance of equatorial actin filament alignment does not require persistent tension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the laser-cutting experiments.

claim: The initial phase of cleavage furrow ingression is mediated by equatorial contraction of a disordered actomyosin network.
source: Our study shows that the initial phase of cleavage furrow ingression is mediated by equatorial contraction of a disordered actomyosin network and that the degree of actin filament alignment within the equatorial cell cortex remains relatively low throughout all stages of furrow ingression, compared to structures like stress fibers or muscle sarcomeres.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the polarization measurements throughout cytokinesis.

claim: The degree of actin filament alignment within the equatorial cell cortex remains relatively low throughout all stages of furrow ingression, compared to structures like stress fibers or muscle sarcomeres.
source: Our study shows that the initial phase of cleavage furrow ingression is mediated by equatorial contraction of a disordered actomyosin network and that the degree of actin filament alignment within the equatorial cell cortex remains relatively low throughout all stages of furrow ingression, compared to structures like stress fibers or muscle sarcomeres.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the polarization measurements throughout cytokinesis.

claim: The late onset and low degree of actin filament alignment within the equatorial cortex suggests a network contraction mechanism underlying cytokinetic cleavage furrow ingression in vertebrate cells.
source: The late onset and low degree of actin filament alignment within the equatorial cortex suggests a network contraction mechanism underlying cytokinetic cleavage furrow ingression in vertebrate cells, yet our data cannot rule out the possibility that at late cytokinesis stages some actin filaments form antiparallel arrays underneath a randomly oriented actin network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: The data cannot rule out the possibility that at late cytokinesis stages some actin filaments form antiparallel arrays underneath a randomly oriented actin network.
source: The late onset and low degree of actin filament alignment within the equatorial cortex suggests a network contraction mechanism underlying cytokinetic cleavage furrow ingression in vertebrate cells, yet our data cannot rule out the possibility that at late cytokinesis stages some actin filaments form antiparallel arrays underneath a randomly oriented actin network.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

claim: Previous studies of actin filament order in mitotic cells relied on conventional widefield epifluorescence polarization microscopy.
source: Previous studies of actin filament order in mitotic cells relied on conventional widefield epifluorescence polarization microscopy, which yields high out-of-focus signal in rounded mitotic cells, restricting accurate quantifications to the flat bottom surface of a cell strain that strongly adheres to the coverslip (Fishkind and Wang, 1993).
evidence: This is a statement about prior methods with citation.

claim: Conventional widefield epifluorescence polarization microscopy yields high out-of-focus signal in rounded mitotic cells.
source: Previous studies of actin filament order in mitotic cells relied on conventional widefield epifluorescence polarization microscopy, which yields high out-of-focus signal in rounded mitotic cells, restricting accurate quantifications to the flat bottom surface of a cell strain that strongly adheres to the coverslip (Fishkind and Wang, 1993).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior methods.

claim: The implementation of fluorescence polarization imaging on confocal microscopes strongly reduces out-of-focus signal.
source: Our implementation of fluorescence polarization imaging on confocal microscopes strongly reduces out-of-focus signal, enabling to study actin network polarization in the native geometry of rounded mitotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical advantage of the current study.

claim: Calibrating the fluorescence anisotropy signal to reference standards with known polarization state informs on the absolute degree of actin filament alignment within the cortical network.
source: Furthermore, by calibrating the fluorescence anisotropy signal to reference standards with known polarization state, our study informs on the absolute degree of actin filament alignment within the cortical network.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Following cytokinetic cleavage furrow initiation, actin filaments progressively align with the cell equator, which strictly depends on myosin II activity.
source: Following cytokinetic cleavage furrow initiation, actin filaments progressively align with the cell equator. This strictly depends on myosin II activity and the degree of actin filament alignment correlates with the local concentration of myosin.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the myosin II inhibition experiments.

claim: The degree of actin filament alignment correlates with the local concentration of myosin.
source: Following cytokinetic cleavage furrow initiation, actin filaments progressively align with the cell equator. This strictly depends on myosin II activity and the degree of actin filament alignment correlates with the local concentration of myosin.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between myosin II localization and actin filament alignment.

claim: The activation of myosin II at the cell equator induces local contractility in a cortical network of randomly oriented actin filaments.
source: In this model, the activation of myosin II at the cell equator would induce local contractility in a cortical network of randomly oriented actin filaments.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: Along the cell equator, each given point experiences counteracting contractile forces from neighboring regions, which would build up high levels of mechanical tension along the circumference of the cell.
source: Along the cell equator, each given point experiences counteracting contractile forces from neighboring regions, which would build up high levels of mechanical tension along the circumference of the cell.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: In the direction perpendicular to the cell equator, highly contractile equatorial cortex regions connect to neighboring regions of lower contractility, which would move toward the equator without building high levels of tension.
source: In the direction perpendicular to the cell equator, highly contractile equatorial cortex regions connect to neighboring regions of lower contractility, which would move toward the equator without building high levels of tension.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: The resulting asymmetric network deformation could explain the filament reorientation toward the direction of the cell equator.
source: The resulting asymmetric network deformation could explain the filament reorientation toward the direction of the cell equator, which might in turn further increase the contractile forces oriented along this direction.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: Filament reorientation might further increase the contractile forces oriented along the direction of the cell equator.
source: The resulting asymmetric network deformation could explain the filament reorientation toward the direction of the cell equator, which might in turn further increase the contractile forces oriented along this direction.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: In C. elegans embryos at the one-cell stage, peaks of myosin contractility and cortical actin filament alignment occur at spatially separate locations.
source: In C. elegans embryos at the one-cell stage, peaks of myosin contractility and cortical actin filament alignment occur at spatially separate locations, whereby long-range cortical flows transduce forces to locally compress the actin filaments before furrowing (Reymann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In C. elegans embryos, long-range cortical flows transduce forces to locally compress the actin filaments before furrowing.
source: In C. elegans embryos at the one-cell stage, peaks of myosin contractility and cortical actin filament alignment occur at spatially separate locations, whereby long-range cortical flows transduce forces to locally compress the actin filaments before furrowing (Reymann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In human cells, peaks of myosin contractility and actin filament alignment co-localize.
source: Our data show that in human cells, peaks of myosin contractility and actin filament alignment co-localize and lateral cortical movement toward the equator does not precede network reorientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the myosin localization and actin alignment measurements.

claim: In human cells, lateral cortical movement toward the equator does not precede network reorientation.
source: Our data show that in human cells, peaks of myosin contractility and actin filament alignment co-localize and lateral cortical movement toward the equator does not precede network reorientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the timing measurements.

claim: During human cell cytokinesis, the actomyosin network aligns directly at the site of highest contractility.
source: This suggests that during human cell cytokinesis, the actomyosin network aligns directly at the site of highest contractility, whereby lateral cortical movements adjacent to the cell equator (Cao and Wang, 1990; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005; Zhou and Wang, 2008) might reflect drag imposed by highest network contractility at the equator.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations to prior observations.

claim: Lateral cortical movements adjacent to the cell equator might reflect drag imposed by highest network contractility at the equator.
source: This suggests that during human cell cytokinesis, the actomyosin network aligns directly at the site of highest contractility, whereby lateral cortical movements adjacent to the cell equator (Cao and Wang, 1990; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005; Zhou and Wang, 2008) might reflect drag imposed by highest network contractility at the equator.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior observations.

claim: In fission yeast cells, actin filaments align before contraction of the actomyosin ring.
source: In contrast to animal cells, fission yeast cells align actin filaments before contraction of the actomyosin ring (Stachowiak et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2006; Vavylonis et al., 2008; Laplante et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on fission yeast.

claim: The alignment of actin filaments before contraction in fission yeast might be due to the high mechanical resistance of the cell wall.
source: This might be due to the high mechanical resistance of the cell wall, requiring a higher degree of actin filament reorientation to generate sufficient tension to ingress the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between fission yeast and animal cells.

claim: Fluorescence polarization microscopy previously showed that septin filaments align with the cell equator during late stages of cytokinesis in budding yeast.
source: Fluorescence polarization microscopy previously showed that septin filaments align with the cell equator during late stages of cytokinesis in budding yeast (DeMay et al., 2011b; Vrabioiu and Mitchison, 2006), but the underlying mechanism has remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Septins bind actin filaments and are required for proper function of the actomyosin ring in Drosophila melanogaster embryos.
source: Septins bind actin filaments and are required for proper function of the actomyosin ring in Drosophila melanogaster embryos (Mavrakis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that asymmetric distributions of mechanical tension might guide both actin and septin filament systems to self-assemble into polarized networks during cytokinesis.
source: Based on our observations, it is tempting to speculate that asymmetric distributions of mechanical tension might guide both actin and septin filament systems to self-assemble into polarized networks during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other filament systems.

claim: Mechanical forces have been suggested to shape other actin-based structures.
source: Mechanical forces have has been suggested to shape other actin-based structures (Fletcher and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior review.

claim: Dendritic actin networks respond to external pushing forces by branching actin preferentially on the convex edge of curved filaments.
source: For example, dendritic actin networks respond to external pushing forces by branching actin preferentially on the convex edge of curved filaments, which orients network growth toward the mechanical force (Risca et al., 2012; Bieling et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The actomyosin ring of vertebrate cells responds to intrinsically generated forces.
source: While these feedback mechanisms rely on external forces, our data suggest that the actomyosin ring of vertebrate cells responds to intrinsically generated forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Actomyosin rings mediate various biological processes, including cellular wound healing and developmental morphogenesis.
source: Given that actomyosin rings mediate various other biological processes, including cellular wound healing and developmental morphogenesis (Schwayer et al., 2016), it will be interesting to further investigate the intricate relationship between contractile forces and actin network organization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.
